title: The Life of the Holy Mother Isidora, Fool-for-Christ
subtitle: From Palladius's account of the Tabennesiot sisterhood
source: Compiled by the editors of Purify from a single principal witness: Palladius of Helenopolis, The Lausiac History, ch. xxxiv 'Concerning a virgin who feigned madness' (English translation by W. K. Lowther Clarke, 1918, public domain). The Synaxarion of Constantinople for the first of May names the heroine of Palladius's chapter Isidora; Palladius himself reports only that she was called by the sisters σαλή, 'the fool,' and gives no other name. The vita preserves Palladius's account in narrative form, naming what he names and stopping where he stops.

sections.title: The sisterhood at Tabennesi
paragraphs: Palladius, writing about the year 419 for the prefect Lausus, devotes one of the chapters of his book to a story that he heard from the desert fathers concerning a virgin in the sisterhood at Tabennesi, in the Thebaid of Egypt. The community had been founded as the women's house corresponding to the great monastery of Saint Pachomius, and it kept the same rule under an abbess of its own; in Palladius's day it numbered about four hundred sisters. They lived in cells and met for the offices in a common church; they laboured at weaving and at the kitchen; and they ate, when they ate, in silence at a common table, after the manner of the men's house across the river.

Among them, Palladius reports, was a sister who hid her ascetical labour under the mask of folly. The sisters called her σαλή, 'the fool,' and the Synaxarion of Constantinople gives her name as Isidora; Palladius gives no name. She wore on her head only a rag instead of the head-covering of the sisterhood, and so was reckoned among the lowest of the house and given the kitchen work.
notes: Palladius's prefatory remarks on the size of the women's house at Tabennesi are in his ch. xxxiii; ch. xxxiv proper opens with the description of the unnamed sister.
The name Isidora is supplied by the Synaxarion of Constantinople (commemoration of May 1) and by the later Orthodox synaxaria that depend on it; the name does not appear in Palladius.

sections.title: The kitchen, the rag, and the silent labour
paragraphs: Palladius describes the manner of her life in the house. She did not, he says, eat at the common table with the sisters; she lived on the crumbs that were swept up after the meals and on the wash-water of the pans she scoured. She was never seen to be at rest. She was never seen to take offence. She was reviled by every sister of the house, struck on the head, sneezed at, scolded, and made the target of every kind of contempt; and she received it all with no answer at all. Palladius adds, in the wording of his translator, that he himself could not say how a single soul had so borne, for so many years, what would have undone a strong body of men in a single day.

She had taken up, the chapter says, this discipline of folly deliberately and as a hidden ascesis: that as one ascetic in the desert flees the world for the love of God, this one had remained in the world but had flown from any honour she might receive. She fasted; she watched; she worked the labour of two; and she carried it under the appearance of being a creature half witted, so that no sister might love her and no soul reckon her among the consecrated.
notes: Palladius, Lausiac Hist. xxxiv. The reading 'she lived on the crumbs and on the wash-water of the pans' is in the Coptic version as well as in the Greek; Lowther Clarke notes the variant in the apparatus of his 1918 edition.

The description of her endurance of insult, and the editorial astonishment of Palladius at it, is the heart of the chapter; the present narrative paraphrases his sense and does not quote any single English translation verbatim.

sections.title: The visit of the Abba Pitiroum
paragraphs: There lived at this time in the desert of Porphyrites a great solitary, Abba Pitiroum, an old man much praised among the brethren for his asceticism. To him an angel of the Lord appeared, Palladius says, and said: 'Why do you think yourself reverend on the strength of these your virtues? Will you have me show you a woman more reverent than yourself? Go down to the women's house at Tabennesi, and there look for one who wears a διάδημα — a crown — on her head; she is greater than you.' The old man, who had not so much as seen a woman's house in many years, took the saying upon himself for an obedience and went down.

He came to the door of the monastery, the chapter goes on, and made his request to the abbess; the rule did not allow a man to enter, but for an anchorite of his reputation an exception was made. The abbess assembled all the sisters and brought them out before him one by one. He looked at every face and saw nothing. He asked, 'are these all?' She said, 'these are all.' He said, 'is there yet another?' She said, 'only the σαλή, the fool, in the kitchen; she does not come out.' He said, 'bring her.' They sent for her; she did not come; they went and fetched her by force.
notes: The location of Pitiroum's cell is given by Palladius as 'in the desert of Porphyrites' (ορος του Πορφυριτου), the porphyry quarries east of the Nile; an old route led from there toward Tabennesi.

The wording of the angel's rebuke, with its question 'why do you think yourself reverend' and its insistence on the διάδημα, is preserved in the Greek text and the Latin Lausiac History both; Lowther Clarke renders διάδημα as 'crown' in his English version of 1918.
That the rule of the women's house did not permit a man to enter, and that Pitiroum was admitted only by virtue of his reputation, is reported in the chapter.

sections.title: The recognition
paragraphs: When the sister was brought, Palladius says, the old man prostrated himself before her and said: 'Bless me, mother.' She prostrated herself in turn and said: 'Bless me, father.' All the sisters were astonished and said to him: 'Abba, do not be deceived; she is a fool.' He said to them: 'You are the deceived; she is amma to me and to you. I will pray that I may be found worthy of her on the day of judgement.' And he told them what had been said to him by the angel.

Then the sisters fell at her feet, every one of them, and confessed in tears the manner of their treatment of her; one had struck her, one had emptied dishwater over her, one had blown her nose in her food. They asked her forgiveness with every kind of word. Palladius reports nothing of her answer, only that she received the embraces of the sisters in silence.
notes: Palladius reports the exchange of prostrations and the words 'bless me, mother' / 'bless me, father' in direct discourse; the present narrative reproduces his sense and does not claim to reproduce either the Greek or any single English translation word for word.
The catalogue of remembered offences (a blow, the dishwater, the food) follows Palladius's chapter; he gives them without sparing the sisters.

sections.title: The departure
paragraphs: Palladius closes the chapter with what he calls a strange and bitter ending. The fame of her sanctity could not be borne by her. She could not endure to be honoured in the place where she had been despised. A few days after the visit of Abba Pitiroum she went out of the monastery quietly, by night, and was not seen again. Whither she went, by what manner of life she lived after, in what country and on what day she fell asleep, Palladius says, no one knew. He himself, who set the story down, professed not to know.
notes: Palladius's final words on the matter, in Lowther Clarke's English of 1918, are nearly: 'where she went, or where she hid, or how she died, no man knows.' The present chapter paraphrases that sentence rather than quoting it.

Later Eastern menologia gave her a name (Isidora) and a feast-day (May 1) but did not undertake to supply what Palladius had refused to supply, namely the place and the day of her repose. The Russian and Athonite traditions reckon her among the holy fools and read her chapter at the trapeza on her commemoration.
